01

The shaper

Wes grew up surfing C Street and started mowing foam in 2009, after a decade of fixing everyone else's dings and wondering why the boards under his feet never quite fit the point at home. He's been shaping full-time since 2014. Everything happens within a mile of the water: he shapes in the shed, a glasser two doors down does the lamination, and the test pilot program is Wes, his neighbors, and whoever's board is next on the list.

He works alone and slowly, on purpose. Each board starts with a conversation — where you surf, what you ride now, what it does that annoys you — and ends with your name and the board's number written on the stringer. He keeps the number in a ledger. Four hundred and eleven so far.

He is not going to scale this. That's the whole idea.

“A machine can cut a board to the thousandth of an inch. It just can't tell you which thousandth matters.”
— Wes, sweeping the shed
02

The boards

Three templates he keeps coming back to, and one he doesn't. The only curves on this page belong to the boards.

The Hull

7′2″ × 21¼″ × 2⅞″ · glassed-on single

The board he'd shape you if you let him decide. Rolled entry, pinched rails, trims like it's late for something. Made for long walls and not pumping.

Usual tint: seafoam

The Pelican

9′6″ × 22″ × 3″ · volan glass

A glider for small days and old knees. Ten strokes in, nose stays dry, glides through flat sections like the bird it's named after. Heavy on purpose.

Usual tint: volan clear

The Ventura Twin

5′10″ × 21¾″ × 2¾″ · keels, swallow

Short, wide, fast. Twin keels foiled by hand from marine ply. The one board on this page that will make you surf worse before it makes you surf better.

Usual tint: ultramarine

And then there's the Scrap — whatever the offcut foam in the corner wants to be that month. You don't order a Scrap. You get offered one.

03

The way it works

  1. The talk

    Half an hour, phone or in the shed. Where you surf, what you weigh, what your current board does that bugs you. Bring the board if you can.

  2. The blank

    Close-tolerance US Blanks foam, picked for your board, stringer and all. Ordered when your number comes up, not before.

  3. The shaping

    Planer, hand screens, sanding blocks, fluorescent side-light. A day of shaping, spread over three, because rails look different in the morning.

  4. The glass

    Resin tint laid by hand at the glass shop two doors down. Tints move; no two come out the same. That's the point.

  5. The wait

    Six months, more or less. He'll text you a photo of the blank when it goes on the racks. Good boards take the time they take.

The list

Write him an email. Say where you surf and what you're after. He answers every one himself, usually in the evening.

Three or four boards go on the racks each month, in the order the emails came in. Get in touch this week and you'll probably be talking dims around January. A deposit holds your number; the rest is due when you pick the board up and turn it over in the sun.

No online checkout. No stock boards. If you need something sooner, he'll happily point you to shapers he rates.
